# The documentation website

These pages are a [Quarto](https://quarto.org) *book* project rendered from the
repository and published to the `gh-pages` branch, from where GitHub Pages serves
them at
[munch-group.github.io/itrails](https://munch-group.github.io/itrails/). Everything
that controls the site lives in the repository, so the documentation is edited,
reviewed and versioned like the code it describes.

## How the site is put together

| File or folder | Role |
|:---|:---|
| `_quarto.yml` | project and book configuration: chapters, theme, options |
| `index.qmd` | the front page |
| `docs/*.qmd` | these documentation pages |
| `notebooks/*.ipynb` | result notebooks, included as chapters |
| `workflow.py` | the workflow, rendered as a chapter |
| `custom.scss` | theme overrides on top of the default Bootstrap theme |
| `references.bib` | bibliography |
| `_book/` | rendered output — generated, not tracked by Git |
| `_freeze/` | cached results of executed documents |

The book is organized into *parts*, each with a list of chapters:

```yaml
book:
  repo-url: "https://github.com/munch-group/itrails"
  repo-actions: [edit, issue, source]
  title: "iTRAILS workflow component"
  chapters:
    - index.qmd
    - part: "User guide"
      chapters:
      - docs/getting-started.qmd
      …
```

`repo-actions` is what puts the *Edit this page* and *Report an issue* links in the
right margin, pointing back at the source file on GitHub.

::: { .callout-important }

A page is part of the book only if it is listed under `chapters`. A `.qmd` file that
is not listed is not rendered at all, and it is easy to add a page and wonder why it
never appears. Add the file to `_quarto.yml` in the same commit.

:::

## Render locally

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi run quarto render          # build the whole site into _book/
pixi run quarto preview         # rebuild and reload in a browser while editing
```

`quarto preview` is the one to use while writing: it watches the files and refreshes
the page on save. To work on a single page without rebuilding everything, pass it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pixi run quarto preview docs/outputs.qmd
```

Quarto is part of the default pixi environment, so no separate installation is
needed.

## Executable content

The project sets `execute: freeze: auto`, which means a document is re-executed only
when its source changes; otherwise the stored result in `_freeze/` is reused. That
keeps rendering fast and, more importantly, keeps the site buildable on a machine
that has neither the cluster nor the data.

Two chapters are not ordinary Markdown:

**`notebooks/example.ipynb`** is executed by the *workflow*, not by Quarto — it is
the last GWF target, and it runs after the results it reads exist. Quarto renders
whatever outputs the notebook carries. If the notebook is committed with its outputs
cleared, the page shows the code without figures, which is the expected state for a
fresh clone that has not run the pipeline.

**`workflow.py`** is rendered directly as a chapter. It is written in the *percent*
format, with `# %%` cell markers and a YAML front-matter cell at the top:

```python
# %% [markdown]
# ---
# title: GWF workflow
# execute:
#   eval: false
# ---
```

`eval: false` is what keeps Quarto from executing the workflow definition while
building the documentation. Writing the workflow this way means the code and its
explanation are the same file, and the rendered chapter cannot drift out of sync with
what actually runs.

## Publishing

`.github/workflows/quarto-publish.yml` renders and publishes on every push to `main`:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

permissions:
    contents: write
    pages: write
```

The job checks out the repository, sets up Python and Quarto, installs Jupyter,
renders the project to HTML, and hands the result to the `quarto-actions/publish`
action with `target: gh-pages`. Jupyter is needed because Quarto starts a kernel to
render `workflow.py`, even though its cells are never evaluated; rendering would
otherwise fail on a clean checkout, where no `_freeze/` cache exists. The action pushes the rendered site to the `gh-pages` branch
using the `GITHUB_TOKEN` that Actions provides automatically — there is no secret to
configure.

For the site to appear, the repository needs **Settings → Pages → Source** set to
*Deploy from a branch*, with the branch `gh-pages` and folder `/ (root)`. That is a
one-time setting per repository.

::: { .callout-tip }

Publishing from CI means `_book/` never needs to be committed, and it is in
`.gitignore` for that reason. If you ever want to publish by hand instead,
`quarto publish gh-pages` does the same thing from a local checkout.

:::

## Adding a page

1. Write `docs/my-page.qmd`, starting with a level-one heading — the heading becomes
   the chapter title in the sidebar.
2. List it under the appropriate part in `_quarto.yml`.
3. Check it with `pixi run quarto render` before pushing; the GitHub Action runs the
   same command, so a render that fails locally fails there too.

Useful conventions used throughout these pages: callout blocks
(`::: { .callout-note }`), fenced code with a filename
(` ```{.bash filename="Terminal"} `), and Markdown tables for option references.
Fenced blocks marked `python` are shown but never executed; only blocks marked
`{python}` would run at render time.
